newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's City Telecom sees room to expand in Asia.
newsitem.headline: HK's City Telecom sees room to expand in Asia.

text.p: City Telecom (HK) Ltd sees huge opportunities to expand its international call services in Asia as markets are opened up under new liberalised trade rules.

City Telecom, a seller of international calling services in Hong Kong, provides international callback services to more than 330,000 individuals and more than 10,000 corporate clients. "The telecommunications market was operated under monopoly in many countries in the past," Ricky Wong, regional director of City Telecom (HK) Ltd, said in an interview on Wednesday.

"However, as 69 countries had committed in the World Trade Orgainsation (WTO) in February that they would gradually open their market on the run-up to the year 2000, it will create huge room for business development," Wong said.

The WTO agreement provides open access to telecom markets around the world, eliminates barriers to cross-border investments among communications carriers, and commits participating countries to establishing pro-competitive regulatory environments for telecom services.
City Telecom is expected to seek a listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in mid-1997 to raise capital for expansion, market sources said.
Wong declined to comment on the listing plan but said the company sees strong future growth.
"We expect our company to continue to achieve double digit growth both in revenue and profit in coming years," Wong said.
The company had revenues of more than HK$500 million for the year ended in August 1996.
City Telecom competes with Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd, the largest and at one time sole provider of international services, as well as with Hutchison Communications and New World Telephone.

Wong said the new competitors were very aggressive in taking market share by reducing their rates. Like its rivals, City Telecom cut rates and found increased traffic volume offset lower prices and led to revenue growth.
But in the future, the competition will focus less on price reduction and more on quality of services, Wong said.

"A price difference of 10 to 20 (HK) cents is relatively insignificant to customers. It (the focus) will be on network quality and stability, in which operating experience is most important," Wong said.
City Telecom's callback services covers more than 200 countries worldwide, and Wong said its network expertise and quality of services would give the company a competitive edge.
Callback services let customers make international phone calls via another country with cheaper charges.
Countries in Asia that had committed to open their markets include Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, Wong said.
Capital will be needed for City Telecom to expand into new markets and for such projects as building switching stations in Japan, Wong added.
City Telecom set up an office in Japan after it obtained a license to provide services there earlier this year.
In Hong Kong, the company is currently renting premises for two switching stations but plans to own at least two over the long run.
Wong said the company's revenue is evenly divided between corporate and individual subscribers.
